content_preview.title: Safari 27 Ships With Safari MCP for AI Coding Agents, Customizable Select Styling, and a Rewritten ECMAScript Module Loader
content_preview.summary: Safari 27.0 folds its Safari MCP developer server into a stable release, adds CSS-styleable select dropdowns, and rewrites the module loader in native C++.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Apple's WebKit team published its developer-facing rundown of Safari 27.0 on September 17, alongside Apple's broader fall 2026 operating-system updates, according to [9to5Mac](https://9to5mac.com/2026/09/17/webkit-blog-breaks-down-whats-new-with-safari-27-for-developers-including-mcp-support/). The release folds the Safari MCP developer server into the stable browser, lets developers fully restyle the native `<select>` dropdown, and ships a from-scratch rewrite of Safari's ECMAScrip...

editor_notes.content_quality: Clear, well-organized News piece (696 words, within the 400-1200 range) covering three distinct Safari 27.0 changes (Safari MCP graduating to stable, restylable native <select>, and the rewritten ESM module loader) plus a new CSS stretch keyword and the <model> element expansion. Overview/What We Know/What We Don't Know/Analysis structure is used correctly; the Analysis section draws a reasonable, non-speculative inference (standards conformance and AI-agent tooling as adjacent priorities) rather than introducing new factual claims.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 4 sources verified by reading the gzipped snapshots directly from disk (sha256 of each decompressed file matches the manifest, confirming snapshot integrity). source-0.html.gz (webkit.org/blog/18325, 'WebKit Features for Safari 27.0', dated Sep 17 2026) confirms: the 58->83 feature-count quote verbatim ('The number of features alone rose from 58 to 83 since the first beta in June.'), the release-notes-length quote verbatim ('Our Safari release notes have never been as long as they are for this version.'), the Safari MCP capability-list quote verbatim ('Safari MCP provides access to the DOM, network requests, screenshots, and console output.'), the appearance: base-select / ::picker-icon / ::checkmark styling claims, the stretch keyword quote verbatim ('The stretch keyword tells an element to fill the available space in the relevant axis.'), the <model> element iOS/iPadOS/macOS availability quote verbatim, the ESM-loader-rewrite quote verbatim ('a complete standards-compliant rewrite of the ECMAScript module (ESM) loader'), and its own internal WWDC fix count of 844 (article correctly attributes the different '850' figure to 9to5Mac's own characterization rather than conflating the two outlets' numbers -- no misattribution). source-1.html.gz (webkit.org/blog/18227, 'Fixing Top-Level Await in Safari', dated Sep 2 2026, matching the article's 'published September 2' claim) confirms the top-level-await bug-explanation quote verbatim ('The promise for the second import shouldn't resolve until after the first import is done evaluating, but due to a bug in the old module loader, it resolves immediately.') and, critically, the exact error-message quote flagged for extra scrutiny: 'Cannot access 'someArray' before initialization.' appears verbatim in the snapshot's reproduction of the console output. This was independently re-verified byte-for-byte against the raw snapshot text, not taken on the submission's word -- no fabrication found. source-2.html.gz (webkit.org/blog/18136, 'Introducing the Safari MCP server for web developers', dated Jul 1 2026, matching the article's 'first introduced in July' claim) confirms the MCP quote verbatim ('By connecting your agent to a Safari browser window, your agent can emulate what your users experience, giving it the information it needs to debug more autonomously, like access to the DOM, network requests, screenshots, and console output.'). source-3.html.gz (9to5mac.com, dated Sep 17 2026) confirms the '850 issues... 525 fixes... WWDC' quote verbatim and the 'Apple's 2027 system releases' quote verbatim. No hallucinated quotes, no misattribution, no unsupported specifics found across any of the four sources.

The headline, summary, and lead claims (Safari MCP going stable, restylable <select>, rewritten ESM loader) are each backed by the webkit.org primary source.
